lines.cap: Your security clearance, part one: submission.
Getting a clearance happens in four chunks: submission, investigation, adjudication, and maintenance.
This part covers everything up to the moment your application reaches DCSA.
Meet Alex. Alex just accepted a job that needs a security clearance.
A clearance is the government's decision that you're eligible for access to classified information.
For contractor employees, that decision belongs to DCSA: the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency.
First, the basics. Only an organization with a facility clearance, or a federal agency, can sponsor you for security clearance eligibility.
And access to classified information is only granted on a need-to-know basis. There are no "just in case" clearances.
If you need access on day one, the process can start pre-employment.
But if the employment is with a private company, that company is required to have you in a cleared position within 45 days of your eligibility being granted.
This video follows a contractor employee like Alex. If you'll work directly for a federal agency, its security office will guide you, and some later steps differ.
Step one. You will need to show proof of U.S. citizenship to your Facility Security Officer, or FSO.
lines.say: Step one. You will need to show proof of U.S. citizenship to your Facility Security Officer, or F S O.

lines.cap: Your FSO can check your documents in person or digitally.
lines.say: Your F S O can check your documents in person or digitally.

lines.cap: Then your FSO will start your investigation request, and you get an email invitation to complete the eApp in NBIS, DCSA's online application.
lines.say: Then your F S O will start your investigation request, and you get an email invitation to complete the e-App in NBIS, D C S A's online application.

scenes.label: You complete the SF 86 in eApp

lines.cap: Step two is yours. In eApp, you complete the SF 86, the Questionnaire for National Security Positions.
lines.say: Step two is yours. In e-App, you complete the S F eighty-six, the Questionnaire for National Security Positions.

lines.cap: It asks where you've lived, worked, and studied, plus foreign contacts, travel, finances, and more.
Most questions look back seven to ten years, so you'll need dates, addresses, and people who can vouch for you.
You should gather records first, so you're prepared for the questionnaire.
Be complete and be honest. Leaving something out can hurt you more than the thing itself.
Before you submit, check for gaps in your timeline, and make sure every date and address is filled in.
You'll also sign release forms and get your fingerprints taken electronically.
Your signed release pages and your fingerprint results are each good for 120 days, so don't let your application sit.
Heads up: a newer form, the Personnel Vetting Questionnaire, is being phased in to replace the SF 86.
lines.say: Heads up: a newer form, the Personnel Vetting Questionnaire, is being phased in to replace the S F eighty-six.

lines.cap: It shortens most look-back periods to five years.
Step three. Your FSO reviews the form for completeness.
lines.say: Step three. Your F S O reviews the form for completeness.

lines.cap: What you disclose isn't shared around the company. The NISPOM strictly prohibits that.
Once the FSO review is complete, it will be released to DCSA, along with your fingerprints.
lines.say: Once the F S O review is complete, it will be released to DCSA, along with your fingerprints.

lines.cap: Step four. DCSA checks that everything is there. If something's missing, it goes back to your FSO, and you fix it and resubmit.
lines.say: Step four. DCSA checks that everything is there. If something's missing, it goes back to your F S O, and you fix it and resubmit.

lines.cap: Missing fingerprints are a common reason a request gets rejected, so they should be taken close to when your form is released.
That's submission: a sponsor with a real need, proof of citizenship, a complete and honest SF 86, releases and fingerprints, and an FSO review.
lines.say: That's submission: a sponsor with a real need, proof of citizenship, a complete and honest S F eighty-six, releases and fingerprints, and an F S O review.
